hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? at the end of a long week, what tells you it’s finally over?
options: then this one is for you. listen.
A meal with people I love
then you already know half of this story. listen.
that counts. listen to how one tradition does it.

steps.line: Friday, just before sunset. In a Jewish home, someone lights the lamps. When the sun goes down, Shabbat, the day of rest, begins.
The Talmud tells that on Friday night, two angels walk each person home from the synagogue. One good angel, and one bad.

steps.q: The angels look inside the home. What do you think they’re checking?
o: How long the person prayed that day
Whether the home is ready for rest
Whether there are guests at the table
steps.why: The lamp lit, the table set, the bed made. Not how holy you were: a home ready for rest.

steps.line: If they find the lamp lit, the table set and the bed made, the good angel says, “May it be like this next Shabbat too.”
And the bad angel, against his will, has to answer, “Amen.”

steps.q: Why is it a little funny that the bad angel has to say amen?
o: He must bless what he’d rather spoil
Amen is the only word he’s allowed
Deep down, he wanted it to go well
steps.why: Amen means “so be it.” A peaceful home is so strong that even the one against it has to agree.

steps.line: If the home is dark and nothing is ready, it goes the other way. The bad angel speaks the wish, and the good angel must say amen.

steps.q: When the home is dark, the bad angel gets to make the wish. What is the story really warning about?
o: A home becomes what it keeps repeating
Angels punish homes that break the rules
Bad angels are stronger than good ones
steps.why: Whatever the angels find, they wish it again for next week. The tale isn’t about punishment; it’s about habit.

steps.line: Today, many people light two candles before sunset, often eighteen minutes early. Many then cover their eyes, say a blessing and look up. Shabbat is here.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Many light the candles, cover their eyes, say the blessing, then look. Why that odd order?
o: To keep the candle smoke out of their eyes
Blessing starts Shabbat; no lighting after
So no one watches them while they pray
steps.why: Usually you bless, then act. Here the blessing starts Shabbat, so you light first, hide the light, bless, and see it as new.

say: here’s what i love. the angels don’t ask how holy you were this week. they look at the lamp, the table, the bed.

in jewish tradition the shabbat light is for shalom bayit, peace in the home: so the people you love can see each other’s faces at dinner. customs differ from family to family, and the light is the same.

steps.q: The rabbis said: if you can afford only one, a Shabbat lamp or a Hanukkah lamp, choose Shabbat. From this lesson, why?
o: It’s commanded in the Torah itself
It brings peace to your own home
steps.why: The Hanukkah lights are for showing the world. The Shabbat light is for the people at your table. Peace at home comes first.

today.say: this friday, before the sun sets, light a candle on your table, and at dinner really look at the faces across from you. learn the blessing, or just watch the flame. your choice.
options: light, then rest. that’s the whole thing.
then light it for you. the light was always for whoever’s at the table.
